title: Income inequality in Brazil since 1980
question: How has income inequality in Brazil evolved since 1980, and what does peer-reviewed research attribute the changes to?
hypothesis: The fall in inequality from 2001 coincided with minimum wage and cash transfer policies, but also with a similar fall in other countries of the region and with labor market changes; no single factor explains the whole fall.
method_description: Description of inequality and poverty series, kept separate by survey (old PNAD and Continuous PNAD), compared with neighboring countries, and a review of studies that decompose the fall in inequality. There is no original causal estimate: shares of the fall attributed to each factor come from the cited studies and depend on their methods.
body:
What the data show

The 1980s: high and rising inequality

According to the old PNAD survey, the Gini of household income per capita was 0.584 in 1981 and reached 0.636 in 1989, the highest value in the series. It was a decade of stagnant income and rising inflation: GDP per capita changed by −5.0% between 1980 and 1990, and consumer price inflation reached 1,430.7% in 1989.

The 1990s: less poverty, same inequality

Between 1993 and 1995, the period of the Real Plan, the poverty rate measured with Ipea's regional lines went from 43.0% to 35.1%. The Gini barely moved: 0.604 in 1993 and 0.601 in 1995. Barros, Henriques and Mendonça (2000) described this as an "unacceptable stability" of inequality.

2001 to 2014: a sustained fall

The old PNAD Gini changed by −0.078 between 2001 and 2014, from 0.596 to 0.518. Over the same period, the poverty rate with regional lines went from 35.8% in 2003 to 13.3% in 2014.

Since 2012: the Continuous PNAD

IBGE's current official series starts at 0.540 in 2012. After the 2015–2016 recession, when GDP per capita changed by −8.1% in two years, the index rose to 0.545 in 2018. In 2020 it went to 0.523 and back to 0.543 in 2021; in those two years income comes from the survey's 5th visit rather than the 1st, because of the pandemic. In 2024 the value was 0.504. The chart shows each year's 95% interval: small differences between adjacent years may not be statistically significant.

Brazil and its neighbors

The fall of the 2000s was not unique to Brazil. Between 2002 and 2014, on the World Bank Gini (0 to 100 scale), Brazil changed by −6.0, Mexico by −1.7 and Colombia by −2.4; urban Argentina changed by −9.2 between 2003 and 2014. When several countries move together, factors common to the region probably matter, alongside national policies.

Inequality beyond income

In 2023 Brazil's HDI was 0.786 and its inequality-adjusted HDI 0.594. The gap is the human development lost to inequality in health, education and income.

What the research attributes

Peer-reviewed studies point to several factors, and none explains the fall alone. The rising minimum wage, targeted transfers such as Bolsa Família and labor market changes, such as lower returns to experience, carry different weights depending on the period, the income measure and the method. Evidence for and against is listed below, each item with its source paper.

evidence_for.text: The 128% real increase in the minimum wage between 1996 and 2018 accounts for 45% of the fall in labor earnings inequality, with muted effects on employment and output, according to an equilibrium model of the labor market.

Conditional cash transfers were less than 1% of total income but, being well targeted, accounted for about 21% of the fall in the Gini in Brazil and Mexico between the mid-1990s and the mid-2000s (accounting decomposition).

Bolsa Família helped reduce inequality and extreme poverty and improved education outcomes, with no negative impact on labor force participation; in health and nutrition the intended effect did not appear, due to supply-side constraints.

evidence_against.text: The fall in labor earnings inequality between 1995 and 2012 is mostly due to lower returns to labor market experience, accounting for 53% of the fall in the labor earnings Gini, more than the falling education premium. This points to labor market changes, not only to specific policies.

With income tax data, top-income concentration is substantially higher than in household surveys and remained broadly stable between 2006 and 2012. The fall measured by surveys may overstate the reduction in overall inequality.

There is suggestive evidence that some families reduced labor supply to become eligible for Bolsa Família, especially female heads of household, according to 2006 PNAD data. This contrasts with studies that find no negative effect on labor force participation.

Considering the whole fiscal system around 2010, when pensions are not treated as transfers, fiscal policy increased poverty in Brazil because of consumption taxes on basic goods, although it always reduced inequality.

limitations: The old PNAD and Continuous PNAD series are not level-comparable and were not spliced. Comparisons across periods should be made within each series.
Household surveys underestimate top incomes; the level and possibly the trend of overall inequality differ with tax data.
Regional comparisons use the World Bank Gini, which for Argentina covers only the urban population, and whose underlying surveys change over time in several countries.
Shares of the fall attributed to the minimum wage, transfers and the labor market come from studies with different periods, income measures and methods; they do not add up.
Temporal coincidence between a policy and the fall in inequality does not show that the policy caused the fall (see the site methodology).
